9:16 竖屏，6 秒，写实手机拍摄质感，固定机位。📷@图片生成 作为开场画面和全片的场景依据。保留📷@图片生成 的室内背景、光线方向、拍摄角度、手部大小、指甲、手链和袖口。右手从第一帧就处在图 1 的位置，手腕从画面右下方斜向伸入，掌心斜朝镜头。📷@图片生成 仅用于参考红白竖条纹纸桶和浅金色爆米花的外观。纸桶出现在图 1 的室内环境中，受光方向与手部一致。 0–2.2 秒　右手空着，拇指和食指轻轻交叠。停一小拍，食指松开，拇指抵住中指。中指快速滑脱，弹向掌根，打出一个清脆的响指。 响指切点　固定机位瞬切。切前最后一帧是空手，切后第一帧是同一只右手已经侧握住完整的爆米花桶。短促的指尖闪光和响指声都落在出桶的这一帧。切点前后，手腕保持相同的画面位置和入画斜线。 2.2–3 秒　右手侧握桶身下半部较窄的位置。虎口贴住桶壁，拇指压在镜头可见的一侧，其余手指从另一侧绕到桶后。握点高于桶底，桶底在手掌下方清楚露出。桶口朝上，停半拍让镜头看清红白条纹和顶部的爆米花。 3–5.2 秒　右手原位持桶。左手从画面左上方伸入，用拇指和食指捏起一颗爆米花，往画外抬走。右手继续扣住桶壁，纸桶保持直立。 5.2–6 秒　画外传来一声清脆的咀嚼声，随后直接切黑。配轻快的无歌词音乐，给响指和咀嚼声留出空间。 避免提前闪光、延迟出桶、纸桶飞入或渐变成形、右手翻成掌心托底、手腕下跳、构图拉远、室内背景变化和手指变形。

items.title: The AI Race is Putting Patients at Risk - Progressive.org
items.summary: Indeed, the most frightening risks involving AI are already moving from theory to capability. Frontier models let non-experts code new applications quickly, and soon it may be possible to use AI to create biological agents that can be weaponized. The White House’s own AI Action Plan warns that AI could create new pathways for bad actors to synthesize dangerous pathogens and calls for stronger screening and national security assessment of AI tools and systems. Anthropic has already said its [...] AI in health care offers many cases that regulatory frameworks should be addressing. A hospital can use AI for patient care and clinical decision support; an insurer for utilization management (e.g., automating care denials); a teenager for mental health advice; a public health department for outbreak detection; and a bad actor for infiltrating a hospital network. Different uses carry different risks and require separate risk-benefit analysis for determining regulatory guardrails. [...] Japan created an AI Strategy Headquarters headed by the prime minister and adopted a national AI basic plan. The United Kingdom and Australia are linking their AI safety institutes in order to better evaluate frontier AI model risks. These systems differ, but they have one thing in common - national AI governance.

items.title: AI Has Entered the Boardroom. Who’s Overseeing It? | Stanford Graduate School of Business
items.summary:
In the survey, 75% of directors said they used AI for research and market analysis, 55% for board prep and material summarization. Other common uses included strategic question generation and competitive benchmarking. Matthys says that board members would ideally like to use AI “to track and summarize board packages and more quickly understand year-to-year trends by using LLM tools rather than reading 80- to 100-page reports.” [...] The sooner the better, the researchers suggest. “Moving too slowly with AI governance means you may miss out on opportunities,” Saripalli says. “The board has fiduciary responsibility for anything that has impact at the product or service level.”

“The risk of not moving is as serious as the risk of AI systems running amok,” Matthys adds, noting how past technological shifts have left unprepared companies behind. “If you don’t keep up, there’s a risk that 20 years from now you won’t exist.” [...] ## In Brief

 A new survey finds that corporate boards are not keeping up with AI governance.
 Directors report that they are discussing and using AI, yet their boards lack a systematic approach to oversight.
 Companies that wait to define AI strategy and audit their AI use risk being left behind.

“We’re trying to change the wheels on the bus while driving it at 100 miles an hour downhill.”

items.title: Chapman Advances Healthcare AI Research and Training | Chapman Newsroom
items.summary:
Totonchy sees the skepticism around AI in higher education as an opportunity.  

“Generative AI quickly gained a negative reputation because it was seen as a tool for cheating,” she said. “That misses the point. These tools can work alongside humans, handling routine tasks so people can focus on analysis and decision-making. The sooner institutions move past resistance, the sooner AI can support that work.” 

STUDENTS PUT AI TO WORK [...] To address bias in clinical decision-making tools, Wang founded the Healthcare AI Initiative (HAI) at Chapman, bringing together researchers working on pressing healthcare challenges. HAI examines ethical questions surrounding AI, including data privacy, and develops equitable machine learning approaches.  

Wang also developed an AI elective within the School of Pharmacy, focused on practical applications for future clinicians. [...] “Every pharmacist has heard the rumors that AI will take pharmacists’ jobs,” Wang said. “But early exposure helps students. As future clinicians, they learn where the real focus should be in relation to AI. That’s something my students learn in this course.”  

Wang also works with students on research projects, extending that learning beyond the classroom. Two PharmD students, Elena Wu ’27 and Harvey Duong ’27, have collaborated with her on studies using AI to analyze large datasets.

items.title: Voters deliver "AI earthquake," rebuking tech and billionaires
items.summary:
Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom.

Why it matters: In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities. [...] The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead-set on winning.

"What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake,"Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios. "Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers." [...] By the numbers: The anti-tech sentiment extended far beyond those states.

   Out of 41 data center measures on the ballot across 10 states, about two dozen proposals designed to restrict or block development appeared to have passed based on initial returns, according to Ballotpedia.
   Ohio hosted the largest share of those ballot fights, and some votes are still forthcoming, including in Arkansas and North Dakota.

items.title: Why New York City is attracting more tech workers
items.summary:
According to Tech:NYC's data, just 35% of NYC's tech employees work at tech companies and startups, while 64% are employed by non-tech companies like banks and media organizations, based on their report published in November 2026.

"When you think about industries like finance, like real estate — industries that have been in New York for a really long time — it has become increasingly clear that technology is driving their work as well," Samuels says. [...] To keep up with artificial intelligence developments, "everyone is hiring" tech workers and consultants, she says: "All these traditional industries are thinking about how they can bring AI into the fold in their own work."

And AI companies are expanding their reach in the city, too: OpenAI leased a 90,000-square-foot office in lower Manhattan, and Anthropic says it plans to double its New York workforce to 1,000 employees in 2026. [...] In today's tech talent market, "the Big Apple is on top," says Lauren Crowley Corrinet, vice chairman at CBRE.

But a big part of New York's tech hiring boom comes from outside the traditional tech sector, according to Julie Samuels, president and CEO of Tech:NYC, a nonprofit representing the city's technology industry.

items.title: China seeks high-tech upper hand in industry carrying 80% of global trade | Reuters
items.summary:
Chinese firms such as self-driving truck maker Westwell and telecoms equipment giant Huawei are packaging smart-port technology for overseas markets. Westwell's driverless trucks now run at Felixstowe, Britain's busiest container port.

Beijing is also drawing on the Belt and Road model that helped it acquire stakes in ports around the world, courting developing countries with technology it says can boost efficiency and trade with the world's second-largest economy. [...] “One key variable for China's speed of automation is the lack of pushback from independent unions who can slow or stop certain kinds of automation in other countries, like the US,” said ‌Kyle Chan, a ⁠fellow in Chinese technology at the Brookings Institution think tank.

China's network of high-tech ports also provides a vast testing ground for technologies its companies can sell abroad. [...] The technology is already accelerating the flow of Chinese goods to global markets. Qianwan says each crane can handle 61 containers an hour, more ​than double the rate at conventional docks.

The United States, by comparison, has been slow to automate in ports, partly due to opposition from labour unions worried about job losses. A 2024 Government Accountability Office report to Congress found that ​the 10 biggest US ports were less automated than their foreign peers.

items.title: The AI Race is Putting Patients at Risk - Progressive.org
items.summary: Indeed, the most frightening risks involving AI are already moving from theory to capability. Frontier models let non-experts code new applications quickly, and soon it may be possible to use AI to create biological agents that can be weaponized. The White House’s own AI Action Plan warns that AI could create new pathways for bad actors to synthesize dangerous pathogens and calls for stronger screening and national security assessment of AI tools and systems. Anthropic has already said its [...] AI in health care offers many cases that regulatory frameworks should be addressing. A hospital can use AI for patient care and clinical decision support; an insurer for utilization management (e.g., automating care denials); a teenager for mental health advice; a public health department for outbreak detection; and a bad actor for infiltrating a hospital network. Different uses carry different risks and require separate risk-benefit analysis for determining regulatory guardrails. [...] Japan created an AI Strategy Headquarters headed by the prime minister and adopted a national AI basic plan. The United Kingdom and Australia are linking their AI safety institutes in order to better evaluate frontier AI model risks. These systems differ, but they have one thing in common - national AI governance.

items.title: AI Has Entered the Boardroom. Who’s Overseeing It? | Stanford Graduate School of Business
items.summary:
In the survey, 75% of directors said they used AI for research and market analysis, 55% for board prep and material summarization. Other common uses included strategic question generation and competitive benchmarking. Matthys says that board members would ideally like to use AI “to track and summarize board packages and more quickly understand year-to-year trends by using LLM tools rather than reading 80- to 100-page reports.” [...] The sooner the better, the researchers suggest. “Moving too slowly with AI governance means you may miss out on opportunities,” Saripalli says. “The board has fiduciary responsibility for anything that has impact at the product or service level.”

“The risk of not moving is as serious as the risk of AI systems running amok,” Matthys adds, noting how past technological shifts have left unprepared companies behind. “If you don’t keep up, there’s a risk that 20 years from now you won’t exist.” [...] ## In Brief

 A new survey finds that corporate boards are not keeping up with AI governance.
 Directors report that they are discussing and using AI, yet their boards lack a systematic approach to oversight.
 Companies that wait to define AI strategy and audit their AI use risk being left behind.

“We’re trying to change the wheels on the bus while driving it at 100 miles an hour downhill.”

items.title: Chapman Advances Healthcare AI Research and Training | Chapman Newsroom
items.summary:
Totonchy sees the skepticism around AI in higher education as an opportunity.  

“Generative AI quickly gained a negative reputation because it was seen as a tool for cheating,” she said. “That misses the point. These tools can work alongside humans, handling routine tasks so people can focus on analysis and decision-making. The sooner institutions move past resistance, the sooner AI can support that work.” 

STUDENTS PUT AI TO WORK [...] To address bias in clinical decision-making tools, Wang founded the Healthcare AI Initiative (HAI) at Chapman, bringing together researchers working on pressing healthcare challenges. HAI examines ethical questions surrounding AI, including data privacy, and develops equitable machine learning approaches.  

Wang also developed an AI elective within the School of Pharmacy, focused on practical applications for future clinicians. [...] “Every pharmacist has heard the rumors that AI will take pharmacists’ jobs,” Wang said. “But early exposure helps students. As future clinicians, they learn where the real focus should be in relation to AI. That’s something my students learn in this course.”  

Wang also works with students on research projects, extending that learning beyond the classroom. Two PharmD students, Elena Wu ’27 and Harvey Duong ’27, have collaborated with her on studies using AI to analyze large datasets.

https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

# OpenAI Third-Quarter Revenue Soars Nearly 50% to $10 Billion

OpenAI’s quarterly revenue hit $10 billion for the first time in the three months ending in September, according to a person familiar with the matter, driven by strong demand for its latest artificial intelligence software. [...] The ChatGPT maker’s revenue increased nearly 50% from the prior quarter and nearly threefold from the same period a year earlier, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The financial details were shared with investors during a call on Tuesday.
